parts.title: How the limits of energy use create a variety of microbes
parts.abstract:
Abstract

The world of microbes is enormously varied. There are a huge number of different kinds of microbes, and they also carry out a great many different chemical processes, called metabolic pathways. Some of these pathways use different starting materials, and some make different end products. Here, we propose that these two facts are directly linked to limits that come from the basic physics of energy, known as thermodynamics. These limits are built into the way microbes grow, because they must get their energy from chemical reactions.

We show that these energy limits can let microbes live side by side even when they use the same starting material but turn it into different end products. We find that this kind of variety, which comes from energy limits, matters most for chemical conversions that release only a small amount of usable energy, called free energy. One example is life without oxygen. In such places, how the numbers of each kind of microbe rise and fall is controlled by energy limits rather than by speed-related factors, such as how fast a microbe can take up its food.

These findings give a general understanding of microbial variety that rests on the first principles of thermodynamics. In this way, they offer an energy-based framework for explaining the microbial variety we see in different natural and human-made environments.
parts.introduction_first: Nature is home to an enormous variety of microbes (Curtis et al., 2002). Scientists who study microbes in their natural surroundings, called microbial ecologists, face a big challenge. One is to count more completely all the different kinds of microbes that exist (Bunge et al., 2013). Another is to explain how this variety comes about and how it is kept going over the long course of evolution. In particular, we need to understand which conditions in the environment, in the microbes' chemistry and in their evolution can create and sustain this variety. That understanding is a necessary first step if we want to understand and control natural communities of microbes (Gudelj et al., 2010; O'Brien et al., 2013), and to design new, human-made communities of microbes (Großkopf and Soyer, 2014).
parts.introduction_rest:
For a long time, one idea has dominated the study of variety in nature. It is called the 'competitive exclusion principle'. It says that once a community has settled into a steady balance, no two species can live side by side if they fill exactly the same role, or niche (Hardin, 1960). A niche is the particular way a species makes a living, including which food it uses and how it uses it.

Scientists have shown this principle in theory for microbes. They did it with mathematical models of a chemostat. A chemostat is a container of liquid food that is kept well mixed, with fresh food flowing in and used liquid flowing out at a steady rate. In these models, the food is a single starting material, called a substrate. The theory predicts that two species can live together only for one special combination of their kinetic parameters. These are numbers that describe how fast each species takes up food and how well it can use it. Outside that one combination, only a single species can survive once things have settled. That species is the one with the highest substrate affinity, meaning it is best at grabbing the food even when there is very little of it (Hsu et al., 1977).

So we would expect one organism to take over each food. We would also expect the number of species we see in nature not to be larger than the number of nutrients or starting materials that limit growth. This idea of exclusion led to a puzzle known as the 'paradox of the plankton'. It asks how so much variety of life can be kept going when there are only a fairly small number of niches (Hutchins, 1961). One way to solve this puzzle is to say that the amount of food changes from place to place and from time to time (Hsu et al., 1977; Pfeiffer et al., 2001; Kerr et al., 2002; MacLean and Gudelj, 2006).

Changes in a single food, across space and time, can certainly add to the variety of microbes. But they cannot explain a different kind of variety. Some species carry out different metabolic pathways that turn the same starting material into different end products (Rodríguez et al., 2008). Even a common food such as glucose can be turned into many different end products, by different species, or even by a single species (Gupta and Clark, 1989). This variety in how microbes break down food adds to the variety of species we see in nature. It is possible that these two kinds of variety are linked.

For example, one idea is that the by-products of a microbe's chemistry (Schink, 1997), and in particular the making of toxic substances (Lenski and Hattingh, 1986), could hold back competing species more than others. They could also hold back the microbe that makes them (De Freitas and Fredrickson, 1978). When such holding back affects species competing for the same food in different ways, it can let them live together on that one food (De Freitas and Fredrickson, 1978; Lenski and Hattingh, 1986).

Arguably, the most basic limit on microbial growth comes from the energy limits of metabolism. Microbes grow by harvesting energy from starting materials as they turn them into end products. So their growth depends on the energy limits of these chemical conversions. In this paper, we look at how these energy limits on the conversions that keep microbes growing are connected to how the numbers of each kind of microbe rise and fall.

We use models of microbial growth that are based on energy limits. With them, we show that the build-up of end products inevitably slows down microbial growth. This slowing can let different species live together, even though they carry out different chemical conversions and use the same starting material. Each conversion has its own energy limits. So species that use these conversions are held back by growth and by their own end products in different ways, and this is what lets them live together.

We find that this effect, which we call 'thermodynamic inhibition', is strongest for reactions that release only a small amount of free energy. There, it outweighs speed-related factors such as how fast a microbe takes up its food. In line with this basic finding, we find that several chemical conversions that matter in real life, as well as conversions of glucose that are possible in theory, fall into the range where energy limits are strong. In this range, different species readily live together on a single food. These findings give an energy-based way to judge the variety of microbes we see in nature.
parts.methods:
## Materials and methods

### An energy-based model of how microbes grow

When a microbe carries out a chemical conversion, the reaction can release or use up free energy. How much free energy it actually releases depends on the conditions. Equation 1 lets us work out this amount under everyday, non-standard conditions.

In Equation 1, R is the gas constant, a fixed number from physics, and T is the temperature. For each compound in the reaction, a is its chemical activity, which is roughly how much of it is available to react, and m is its stoichiometric coefficient, the number of molecules of that compound that the reaction makes or uses up. The letter i stands for the products and j for the starting materials. The equation also includes the change in free energy under biological standard conditions. These are a set of agreed reference conditions: a concentration of 1 m for every dissolved substance, a pressure of 1 atm, a temperature of 25 °C, and a pH of 7 (neutral, neither acidic nor alkaline).

We use an energy-based model that other researchers proposed earlier (Hoh and Cord-Ruwisch, 1996). It captures how microbes grow when there is no oxygen and little energy is available. The model builds on the work of Haldane (1930) on reversible enzyme kinetics. Enzymes are the proteins that speed up chemical reactions, and a reversible reaction is one that can run in both directions, forwards and backwards. From this work, the model works out a formula for how fast a microbe grows.

In this formula, the energy available from the reversible reaction depends on how much of each starting material and product is present, as given in its general form in Equation 1. The model has two constants. K is the half saturation constant for how fast the starting material is used up. It tells us how much starting material is needed for the reaction to run at half its top speed. The other constant, kr, is the ratio of the fastest possible forward reaction rate to the fastest possible backward reaction rate (Hoh and Cord-Ruwisch, 1996).

Because the model treats microbial growth as a reversible enzyme reaction, it assumes that the speed of this reaction can be taken as the growth rate. In reality, the energy available from the reaction would have to be spent on driving the reaction itself, as well as on growth and on keeping the cell alive. Later studies have tried to deal with this by proposing other models. These models link the energy used in breaking things down (catabolism) with the energy used in building things up (anabolism) (Kleerebezem and Stams, 2000; Jin and Bethke, 2003, 2007; Rodríguez et al., 2008).

In our study, any of these more complex models could be used without changing our key conclusion. That conclusion is that energy limits can lead to a variety of microbes even when they all use the same starting material (see Supplementary Text). When we tried these other models, the conclusions about how speed-related factors and energy limits work against each other (Figure 5) changed only in their numbers. The change depended on exactly which model we chose, because each model says something different about how much of the free energy from a reaction goes into growth rate and how much goes into building new cell material. The results we present are therefore a cautious, low estimate.

### A speed-based model of how microbes grow, without energy limits

To compare with the energy-based model, we also use a model that looks only at speed. It was first developed by Monod (1949). This model describes microbial growth with a formula based on measurements, and it leaves out the effects of energy limits. The speed of a microbe's chemical reactions is given by this formula.

This formula also comes out of the energy-based model (Equation 2) when the free energy released by the growth reaction is very negative. In that case, the term exp(ΔGrxn) is so small that it is close to zero.

### Modelling how two kinds of microbes grow in a chemostat using the same starting material

A chemostat is a container of liquid in which fresh food is added and liquid is removed at a steady rate, so that the amount of liquid stays the same. We imagine two kinds of microbes, X1 and X2, living in a chemostat and eating the same starting material, S. We assume that X1 turns S into a different end product, P1, and that X2 turns it into a different end product, P2. No microbes are added to the chemostat from outside. The starting material in the incoming liquid has a concentration of S0. The dilution rate, λ, is how fast the liquid is replaced, measured per hour.

With these symbols and a chosen model of microbial growth, we can write ordinary differential equations (ODEs). These are equations that describe how the amount of each kind of microbe changes over time. To find the amounts of each kind of microbe at steady state, we set the left side of each equation to zero. Steady state means that the amounts are no longer changing. In particular, we can use the steady-state conditions of the second and third equations to get a condition for the steady state.

In this condition, a bar over a symbol means the amount at steady state. For the speed-based model, this condition can only be met if ν1 × Y1 = ν2 × Y2. Here ν is the reaction speed of each kind of microbe, given by Equations 2 or 3, and Y is the yield, meaning how much new cell material is made from each unit of food. This condition can only be met in one way: if the yields, top growth rates and uptake rates of the two microbes are set to a particular combination, or if all of these are the same. That second case means X1 and X2 are really the same kind of microbe (Hsu et al., 1977). With any other set of values, the kind of microbe that is less good at taking up the starting material will be washed out of the chemostat (Hsu et al., 1977).

For the energy-based model, the steady-state condition leads to a different equation.

We assume that kr1,2 = 1, so the fastest forward and backward reaction rates are equal. We also assume that K1 and K2 are much larger than the amount of starting material at steady state. With these assumptions, we can rearrange the equation to get a condition for the steady state.

In this condition, A is a combined value made from the model's settings. So the two kinds of microbes can live side by side at steady state if their speed-related settings and the free energy changes of their chemical conversions fit together in the right way. The free energy changes of these conversions depend on how much of each starting material and product is present. This means the two kinds of microbes can live side by side across a wider range of changing conditions than in the speed-based model.

We also want to get a sense of how the share of each kind of microbe at steady state depends on the amounts of the end products. To do this, we make a strict assumption: the two kinds of microbes have the same yield, top growth rate and uptake rate. This could be true just after one kind of microbe splits into two new kinds. In that case, A = 1. We can then put Equation 1 into the simplified Equation 7. This gives a link between the amounts of the end products at steady state and the standard free energy changes of the chemical conversions.

The amounts of the end products at steady state are linked to the amounts of each kind of microbe (see Equation 4 and Supplementary Text). So the link in Equation 8 also applies to the amounts of the microbes. We conclude that two kinds of microbes with the same speed-related settings will live side by side at steady state. How many of each there are depends on the standard free energy changes of the chemical conversions they use, as given in Equation 8.

### Finding chemical conversions that start from glucose

We wanted to see how common chemical conversions are that release only a small amount of free energy. To do this, we looked at fermentation reactions that start from glucose. Fermentation is a way of breaking down food without oxygen. We used only reactions that are balanced, meaning that the atoms on both sides of the reaction match. Each reaction also involved 12 other common compounds.

We made every possible reaction among these compounds, with glucose always as a starting material. To do this automatically, we set a range of allowed values for the stoichiometric coefficient of each compound. A negative value means the compound is a product, and a positive value means it is a starting material. A computer then tried every combination of values within these ranges to make all the possible reactions.

The 13 compounds we used, with their ranges (lowest value; highest value), were: glucose (−1; −1), lactate (0; 2), acetate (0; 3), CO2 (−6; 6), formate (0; 3), pyruvate (0; 2), acetaldehyde (0; 2), ethanol (0; 2), H2 (0; 6), H+ (0; 12), water (−6; 6), butyrate (0; 2) and methane (0; 6).

As an example, homolactic fermentation of glucose, which turns glucose into lactate, would be written as this list of values for the compounds: [−1, 2, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2, 0, 0, 0]. We made every possible list of values within the ranges (that is, every combination of values). We then checked each one to see whether it was chemically balanced and whether the atoms matched up.

To check this, we multiplied each list by a table of numbers. The table holds how many carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atoms each molecule has, as well as its electric charge (see Supplementary Table S1). For a reaction to be balanced, the result of this multiplication must be zero. We treated the balanced reactions as ones that could happen in living things. We then worked out the free energy change of each one, assuming biological standard conditions (1 m, 1 atm, 298.13 °K, pH = 7). For this we used published values of the energy stored in each compound (Thauer et al., 1977).

The full list of reactions from this analysis is given in Supplementary Table S2. A MATLAB computer program that carries out these steps is provided in Supplementary File. It can also be found at http://osslab.lifesci.warwick.ac.uk/?pid=resources.
parts.results:
## Results

To understand how the chemistry inside a cell is linked to the way microbes live together, we start from the basic physics of energy that makes microbial growth possible. A microbe grows by harvesting the free energy that is released when it carries out chemical conversions. Like any other chemical reaction, these conversions follow the rules of thermodynamics. The free energy change of a reaction is the difference between the free energy of the products and the free energy of the starting materials. This is the most energy, in theory, that a microbe can get from breaking down a starting material to build its own body, under standard conditions. Standard conditions mean that every dissolved substance has a concentration of 1 m, the pressure is 1 atm, the temperature is 25 °C and the pH is 7. When the real concentrations differ from these, we can work out the energy that is actually available for growth, which we call ΔGrxn, using Equation 1. In reality, a microbe would get less energy for growth than this maximum. That is because it has to spend some energy on building its body and on keeping itself alive (Thauer et al., 1977; Hoh and Cord-Ruwisch, 1996; Jin and Bethke, 2007; Rodríguez et al., 2008). We discuss this further below.

### Energy limits let several kinds of microbes live on the same starting material

To take these energy limits, described by Equation 1, into account, we use a growth model based on thermodynamics (Hoh and Cord-Ruwisch, 1996) (see Materials and methods). Earlier work showed that this model explains microbial growth better than models based only on speed-related factors, especially in places without oxygen where little energy is available, because there the effects of energy limits are expected to be stronger (Hoh and Cord-Ruwisch, 1996). In this model, the growth rate of each kind of microbe depends on two things. One is a speed-related factor, which depends on how fast the microbe takes up its food. The other is an energy factor, which depends on the free energy of the reaction that turns the starting material into the products (see Equation 2). We also tried other thermodynamic models, and they did not change the main conclusions of our study (see Materials and methods and Supplementary Text).

We first use this growth model for the simplest and most idealised case: two kinds of microbes living on a single starting material in an evenly mixed environment. This situation can be set up in an ideal chemostat, a container where fresh food flows in and the liquid, along with the microbes and their products, is diluted at a steady rate. We can describe a chemostat with ordinary differential equations, which are equations that tell us how the amounts of each substance change over time (see Materials and methods). Earlier chemostat models treated growth as depending only on how fast microbes take up their food. From these models came the exclusion principle. If two kinds of microbes have the same top growth rate and the same growth yield (the amount of new body built from each unit of food), then only one of them can survive in a chemostat with a single starting material. That survivor is the one that takes up its food fastest (Hsu et al., 1977) (Figures 1a and b). When the speed-related settings of the two microbes are allowed to differ, there is only one particular combination of top growth rate and food uptake rate at which both can live together (Hsu et al., 1977).

When we model two kinds of microbes with the same growth, uptake and yield settings using the thermodynamic growth model, we find something different. Both can live together on a single starting material, and this can be a stable state, as long as they turn it into different end products (Figures 1c and d). The reason is simple. In the thermodynamic model, growth depends not only on yield and uptake, but also on the free energy change of the conversion. This free energy change depends on the concentrations of the starting material and the products (Equation 1). So it keeps changing each microbe's growth rate as the concentration of its own products changes. In particular, as products build up, less free energy is left for the microbe to spend on growing. This is a bit like each microbe holding back its own growth. In the end, it leads to a balance in how much of the starting material each microbe uses, among the different microbes that make different end products (Figure 1d). The result is a steady state that keeps shifting over time. In it, how common each microbe is depends on the free energy of the pair of starting material and product that it uses, that is, on its breakdown reaction. More precisely, we can show that for the simple case of two microbes on a single starting material, with all their speed-related settings for uptake, top growth rate and growth yield equal, the ratio of how common the two are at the steady state is linked to the free energy of their breakdown reactions (see Materials and methods and Equation 8). This result also carries over easily to many kinds of microbes living together on a single starting material in a chemostat, as long as each can carry out a different breakdown reaction that is chemically possible.

**Figure 1.** How the numbers of two kinds of microbes change over time when they live on a single starting material in a chemostat, modelled with a speed-based model (a, b) and with a thermodynamic model (c, d) (see Materials and methods). Panels (b and d) show the share of the total body mass made up by microbe X1 (dashed line), with vmax=1 and K=0.1, and by microbe X2 (solid line), with vmax=1 and K=0.01. The total body mass is scaled to 1. The chemostat settings are λ=0.1 and S0=1000.

### Living together because of energy limits matters most for conversions that release little free energy, and such conversions are common in nature

We now look at what happens to how common each microbe is as the gap between the free energy changes of the two reactions they use gets bigger. As Equation 8 predicts, the ratio of how common the two are grows exponentially in favour of the microbe that uses the reaction with the larger free energy change (the more negative one) as the gap widens (Figure 2). In other words, living together because of energy limits is always possible in theory. But as the gap between the two reactions grows beyond about 50 kJ (mol Substrate)−1, the microbe whose reaction releases less free energy becomes more and more rare, until its numbers are tiny compared with the other (Figure 2). It is important to note that our thermodynamic model leaves out the energy that microbes spend on building their bodies and on keeping themselves alive. So it gives a cautious, low estimate of this energy range. Also, more complex chemical reactions that make several products can widen the range in which microbes can live together (see Supplementary Text).

**Figure 2.** A double logarithmic plot, where each step along both axes multiplies the value by the same amount, showing how the difference in free energy (dΔG) between the two reactions affects the ratio of the body masses of the two microbes X1 and X2 at the steady state. Both grow in a chemostat on the same starting material but make different waste products (according to Equation 8).

For the reasons above, Figure 2 gives a cautious estimate of the energy gap between breakdown reactions that would still let microbes live together in large numbers. Even so, it is worth asking how much this range of energy gaps matters in nature. In particular, are there chemically possible breakdown reactions that different microbes can use on the same starting material, with free energy changes within about 50 kJ (mol Substrate)−1 of each other? To answer this, we gathered the free energy changes of known microbial breakdown reactions that support growth, using published tables. We focused on reactions that happen in places without oxygen, such as sediments, animal guts and anaerobic digesters, which are tanks where microbes break down waste without oxygen (Table 1) (Thauer et al., 1977; Conrad et al., 1986; Seitz et al., 1988; Schink, 1997; Kleerebezem and Stams, 2000; Walker et al., 2009; Dolfing, 2013; Worm et al., 2014). As Table 1 shows, many of these reactions are within 20–100 kJ of each other (Figure 3).

We wanted to go further and allow for any possible bias in the known reactions that support microbial growth. So we also used a computer to work out every chemically possible reaction within a set range of conditions. Our aim was to build a large set of reactions in which glucose is broken down by fermentation (see Materials and methods). This thorough search of all the conversions from glucose that are possible both in terms of energy and in terms of the chemical recipe (the stoichiometry) showed that most of these reactions have free energy changes within 50–100 kJ (mol Substrate)−1 of each other (Figure 3).

### Microbes that break down propionate show how products affect living together

To show the effect of energy limits on living together with a concrete example, we look at three different reactions in which microbes break down propionate without oxygen (Table 1). Two of these reactions are known to happen at the same time in rice paddy soils without oxygen (Gan et al., 2012), which means that the microbes carrying them out live side by side in these places. The two reactions have different standard free energy changes. They also differ in the amounts of waste products they make, especially in how much hydrogen gas (H2) they produce. Under standard conditions, with a hydrogen pressure of 1 atm, none of the reactions releases energy. But under more realistic conditions, with starting materials and products at concentrations of a few thousandths of a mole per litre (millimolar), there is a hydrogen pressure at which any of the three reactions will release energy.

What is interesting is that, across the full range of hydrogen pressures that microbes can live with, the reaction that releases the most energy per propionate is held back at a lower hydrogen pressure than the other two (Figure 4). This comes from the chemical recipe of the reactions. The reaction that releases the most energy at low hydrogen pressures also makes the most hydrogen: for every 1 propionate it uses, it makes 7 hydrogen molecules. In other words, the hydrogen that this reaction itself quickly produces builds up and removes its energy advantage at low hydrogen pressures. This example shows again that microbial growth will be dominated by the energy of the reactions that support it. As products build up, this can then lead to new ways in which microbes with competing reactions can live together, and to more variety.

**Figure 4.** The free energy of three propionate-breaking reactions (from Table 1), per propionate, at different hydrogen pressures in the surroundings. Each reaction makes hydrogen as a by-product, and the line style shows the ratio of propionate to hydrogen in that reaction (see the legend). We calculated the free energy at pH=7, with 1 mmol l−1 of propionate, acetate and HCO3− in the surroundings, and with the hydrogen pressures shown on the x axis.

### Energy limits dominate for conversions that release little energy, but speed-related factors can easily win out for conversions that release a lot

So far, we have looked at microbes living together only because of differences in their chemical conversions and the energy limits that follow. In reality, microbes can differ in many traits that shape their chemistry and growth. Among these, speed-related traits, such as how fast they take up their food, could be especially important for keeping many kinds of microbes around, as mathematical studies of the exclusion principle have pointed out (Hsu et al., 1977). To look into this, we went back to the case of two microbes on a single starting material, this time without assuming that they take up their food at the same speed. We let one microbe use a conversion that releases slightly more energy, and then changed how fast it takes up its food. In other words, we explored whether speed-related factors can work against the effects of energy limits when microbes compete and live together.

As we expected, speed-related factors can work against energy limits. A microbe that uses a conversion releasing more energy can become the rare one if it takes up its food more slowly (Figure 5). We find that this effect of speed winning out over energy becomes stronger as the free energy changes of the conversions used by the two microbes get larger. This follows directly from the thermodynamic growth model (Equation 2). As the free energy changes get larger, the effects of products building up become tiny, and growth comes to depend more and more on how fast the microbe takes up its food (for further analyses, see Supplementary Text).

**Figure 5.** A computer simulation showing how the affinity for the starting material (the setting K in Equation 2) and the free energy of the conversion affect the mix of the two microbes at the steady state. The colours show the share of the total body mass made up by microbe X2. The y axis shows K1, the K of microbe X1, while K2, the K of microbe X2, is fixed at 10 × 10−6. The x axis shows the free energy of the conversion for microbe X1, while that of microbe X2 is always set 5 kJ (mol Substrate)−1 lower than that of X1, meaning it is more favourable in terms of energy.
parts.discussion:
## Discussion

We built a model of microbial growth based on the basic physics of energy, and we used it to study how the numbers of different kinds of microbes rise and fall when they compete and whether they can live side by side. The model follows the basic rules of energy conservation and thermodynamics as microbes turn food into the energy they need to grow. Its key result is this: when different kinds of microbes use different chemical conversions, they can live side by side on a single starting material, even in an environment that is the same everywhere.

In this situation, how common each kind of microbe becomes depends on how much usable energy (free energy) its chemical conversion releases. We measure this in kilojoules per mole of starting material, written kJ (mol Substrate)−1. A mole is simply a fixed, very large number of molecules, so this unit tells us how much energy is released for each mole of food used up. We find that kinds of microbes using conversions that release about 50 kJ (mol Substrate)−1 less energy than the conversion that releases the most would still live side by side, and would each make up a large share of the community. When we looked at chemical conversions that are already known, or that are possible in principle, we found that this range of energy values is biologically important, because many of the chemical reactions known to keep microbes growing fall within it. This suggests that a large amount of microbial variety on a single starting material could first have arisen from energy limits, or is still being kept going by them.

As the usable energy released by a conversion gets larger, however, we find that speed-related factors take over from energy limits in controlling how the numbers of microbes rise and fall. One example is how fast a microbe can take up its food. So we would expect that any change in these speed-related settings, for example through evolution, would easily upset the variety that energy limits create when conversions release a lot of usable energy. This is not true for conversions that release only a little usable energy. There, we find that two kinds of microbes using conversions that release −20 and −25 kJ (mol Substrate)−1 can still live side by side, even if one needs ten times more food than the other before it starts to grow at half its top speed (Figure 5). This measure is called the half saturation constant.

We stress that our predictions about which energy ranges allow microbes to live side by side are cautious estimates. This is because our model assumes that all of the usable energy from a conversion goes into making the microbe grow faster (Hoh and Cord-Ruwisch, 1996). In reality, some of this energy would have to go into building the cell's own parts and into other jobs that keep the cell running (Kleerebezem and Stams, 2000; Jin and Bethke, 2003; Rodríguez et al., 2008). As a result, even conversions that release more usable energy could fall into a range where energy limits hold growth back, and this could open a window for variety driven by energy limits to appear.

Our model looks at the energy side of microbial growth by treating growth as one overall chemical reaction, such as turning glucose into acetate. In reality, a cell's chemistry is made up of many reactions that end in a final product. So the usable energy released by the overall reaction is shared out among all the individual reactions, and some of it has to be spent just to keep these reactions running fast enough (Flamholz et al., 2013). This means that not all of the usable energy from the overall reaction can go into making the microbe grow faster, as we assume here. Our estimates of how energy limits hold growth back could therefore apply over a wider range of conditions, that is, even to overall reactions that release more usable energy than we studied here. In future work, it may be possible to include the different chains of reactions used by different kinds of microbes, to get a more accurate model of how their growth is controlled by energy. Indeed, researchers are already doing studies like this to compare different chains of reactions (Flamholz et al., 2013) and to check whether they can work under different conditions (González-Cabaleiro et al., 2013; Cueto-Rojas et al., 2015).

The energy limits we describe here act in a similar way to the way waste products of a microbe's chemistry can hold back the growth of other microbes (De Freitas and Fredrickson, 1978; Lenski and Hattingh, 1986). But it is important to note that energy limits do not hold back growth directly. Instead, they come from the natural push of the chemical reaction that keeps a microbe growing towards a balance, called chemical equilibrium, where the reaction stops changing. So each kind of microbe is affected by the build-up of its own products. This built-in energy mechanism therefore punishes the fastest-growing microbes first, and in this way it favours many different chemical conversions living side by side in the environment. The products of these different conversions can then be used as a source of energy, either by the same kind of microbe or by a different one. This is an example of 'niche creation', where one microbe's waste becomes another's food, and it could lead to even more microbial variety and to new ways of interacting as microbes adapt. Indeed, communities of microbes that live without oxygen often contain many such linked chemical conversions (Schink, 1997, 2002).

Our findings suggest that microbes can readily live side by side when the chemical reactions that support their growth release only a little usable energy. A direct experiment to test this idea would be to grow two different kinds of microbes, or specially marked versions of the same kind, on a single starting material. The kinds of microbes and the starting material should be chosen so that each kind can only use conversions that release a little usable energy. Such an experiment could be run in a chemostat, a container where fresh food is added and used-up liquid is removed at a steady rate, so that the amount of food stays constant. It could also be run in a closed container with no fresh food added, called a batch, to test whether each kind can invade the other when it starts out rare. Examples would include growth without oxygen on propionate or glycerol, where different chains of reactions are known to exist.

More broadly, our study suggests that environments where microbes can mainly grow using conversions that release a little usable energy should hold more variety in their chemical conversions than environments where they can use conversions that release a lot. This idea could be tested using the growing amount of metagenomics data, which is the genetic information of all the microbes in a sample, collected from different environments. Examples of the first type of environment would include anaerobic digesters (tanks where microbes break down waste without oxygen), animal guts, wet soils and the mud on the seafloor in very productive parts of the ocean. In these environments, there is a lot of food, but there are no strong oxidising agents such as oxygen or nitrate, which are substances that microbes often use to get energy from their food. As a result, waste compounds build up to high levels. So we expect that microbial growth in these environments is mainly limited by how little usable energy the particular conversions each kind of microbe uses can provide. Microbes can get around this limit by evolving the ability to turn the same food molecule into different waste products. In this way they can keep growing by making products that are only present at very low levels in the environment, and so escape being held back by the build-up of their own products. This situation is like a river flowing from the mountains to the sea. On its steeper parts, the river stays within a single valley, but as it runs over the flat land near the coast it starts to wind and form many small rivers in a delta.
